A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same MultiSocial research. Their main text, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–F support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 17 detectors, cross-language and cross-platform experiments, dataset analyses, and cross-domain results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds original evaluations of text-quality judges, generated-text quality, and dataset composition.

M1.justification: The three-iteration paraphrasing procedure, generation parameters, detector architectures, and fine-tuning procedures remain unchanged. The new LLM judges provide supplementary dataset evaluation.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds METAL's human-rated texts in ten languages for validating text-quality judges. MultiSocial's 22-language, five-platform detection coverage and the MULTITuDE cross-domain evaluation remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The 17 detection comparators are retained. New Table 13 compares five open quality judges—Llama-3.1, Phi-3.5, Qwen2, Aya-23, and Gemma-2—with GPT-4 reference scores explicitly taken from METAL.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a substantial quality-evaluation protocol: weighted-F1 agreement with METAL human judgments, two quality scales scored from 0 to 2, three selected judges assessing 4,012 generation-approach samples, and majority-voted ratings for 1,752 final-dataset samples. It also adds automatic toxicity, topic, and genre classification. Existing detection protocols are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.4–B.5 examine quality across paraphrasing iterations, generators, and languages, and characterize toxicity, topics, and genres. Table 11 adds paired text examples exposing residual language-label errors. These substantially extend the analyses beyond the retained similarity studies, architecture-group ablation, and cross-domain experiments.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 newly reports inter-judge agreement, with average pairwise Pearson correlations of 0.82 for generation-approach samples and 0.69 for final-dataset samples. Existing detector confidence intervals and paired t-tests remain unchanged; no additional detector run counts or seed settings are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds judge-validation and text-quality results in Tables 13–15, approximately 8% predicted toxicity, and topic/genre distributions. Existing detection scores match, including Llama-3-8B's 0.9769 AUC ROC and 0.8696 MacroF1 in v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 4. The additions constitute substantial new results without a demonstrated detection-performance change.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory or proofs, and v2 adds no mathematical derivations or revised formal assumptions. Its new quality rubrics and agreement metrics are empirical evaluation procedures.

C1.justification: The benchmark novelty claims and central findings about successful fine-tuning and platform-dependent transfer remain. Contributions are reordered, and the conclusion adds a 27% transfer-gap example already supported by v1 Table 26, without changing the core claim's scope.

C2.justification: v2 explains higher generated-text quality ratings through differences between formal model training text and informal human posts. It also acknowledges residual language-label errors, platform imbalance in quality assessment, and the indicative accuracy of automatic bias classifiers. Existing principal interpretations and limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the IMGTB implementation, newly documents anonymization of usernames, emails, and phone numbers, and reports approximately 1,800 GPU-hours on three A100 40GB GPUs for quality evaluation. It replaces the anonymous resource pointer with separate GitHub code and Zenodo dataset links. Existing generation and training hyperparameters remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting METAL, LLM evaluation, toxicity/topic/genre classification, and IMGTB, including positioning open judges against METAL's API-based models. The related-work comparison with earlier text-detection datasets and the principal novelty positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained. Edits reorder the contribution list, move the generator-similarity discussion into Section 3, introduce Appendices B.4–B.5, and make localized explanatory, wording, and capitalization changes.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual presentation with a full-page paired-example table, three judge/quality-evaluation tables, and topic and genre charts. It also relocates v1 Table 10 to the main text as Table 3, reformats the language map, and adjusts table placement and captions.

improvement.justification: The new examples, human-referenced judge evaluation, and quality and bias analyses make the benchmark's construction and limitations easier to assess. Resource and implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. The benefit is limited by small quality-assessment samples and reliance on automatic judges and imperfect classifiers; the central detection evidence remains unchanged.
